The work, "The twofold copia of words and arguments in a double commentary" (Latin: De duplici copia verborum ac rerum), is known for its mastery and freshness in forming and expressing thoughts, especially for "forensic oratory." Its full title is a joke, perhaps, as it is famously known for including 147 variations on "Your letter pleased me very much" and 203 variations on "Always, as long as I live, I shall remember you." The first part of the book is about verborum (words), while the second part is about rerum (arguments).

In the novel, Nan's first-person account of her own past, told many years later, transcends the usual rites of passage that most mainstream stories focus on, leaving aside the importance of birth, marriage, reproduction, and death. This transcendence of time is evident in the narration of the novel.

When it comes to the television adaptation of the book, Waters was quite surprised that the BBC chose to produce and broadcast a television adaptation that faithfully followed the relish and detail of sexual escapades in the book. Stirling thoroughly enjoyed it.
